idiom_name: iter.Seq[T] closures composed with slices/maps helpers and iter.Pull
implementation_notes: Go 1.23 added range over function types and the iter package: an iterator is a function that passes successive elements to a yield callback (iter.Seq[T]), so stages compose as closures and are consumed directly by for ... range, element by element, with no intermediate slices. iter.Pull converts a push iterator into next/stop functions when a loop needs manual control, and slices.Values/slices.Collect are the adapters to and from slices at explicit boundaries. The composition helpers (map/filter) are hand-written because the standard library ships only the adapters, so this is idiomatic Go rather than a framework.
pitfalls: A channel-per-stage pipeline (goroutine plus chan between stages) is the Go anti-pattern here: every stage buffers and schedules, goroutines must be shut down explicitly, and it is backpressure plumbing rather than fusion.
range-over-func iterators are push-based: early break works only because yield returns false and the iterator honours it; an iterator that ignores the return value keeps producing.
Ending a pipeline in slices.Collect materializes it once - keep that call at a real boundary, never between stages.

variants.name: Hand-written single pass (pre-1.23 baseline)
variants.idiom_name: one explicit for loop with the stages inlined in order
variants.implementation_notes: Without range over function types - or when a transformation is used exactly once - the Go idiom is one explicit loop over the data with the stages inlined in order: no intermediate slices, no goroutines, no adapters. This is classic fusion performed by hand, and it stays the right answer for one-off pipelines and for hot loops where per-element closure calls would be measurable.
pitfalls: Inlining everything couples the stages again; when two places need the same transformation, extract a named function or a slice of stage functions.
Preallocating the output slice with make([]T, 0, len(in)) is a materialization decision - only do it at a real boundary.
